title: Standard error reduction: effect of quadrupling sample size
scenario_markdown: A precision CNC milling line produces aerospace titanium pins whose diameters have a known process standard deviation of $\sigma = 20.0\ \mu\text{m}$. A quality assurance team initially draws a random sample of $n_1 = 25$ pins to estimate the mean pin diameter $\mu$. To tighten their estimate, management approves quadrupling the sample size to $n_2 = 100$ pins.
assumptions: Titanium pin diameters are independent and identically distributed
Process standard deviation sigma is stable at 20.0 microns
Sampling fraction is negligible (infinite population assumption, FPC not required)
source_refs: Course Module 4: Sampling Distributions and Confidence Intervals

approval.notes: Verified mathematical derivations: SE_1 = 20.0 / sqrt(25) = 4.0 um; SE_2 = 20.0 / sqrt(100) = 2.0 um. Ratio SE_1 / SE_2 = 4.0 / 2.0 = 2.0. Quadrupling n reduces standard error by factor sqrt(4) = 2. Excel formulas: =20/SQRT(25) and =20/SQRT(100).

stages.prompt_markdown: Calculate the standard error of the sample mean $\sigma_{\bar{x}}$ for the initial sample of $n_1 = 25$ pins.

options.hint_markdown: Standard error divides the standard deviation by the square root of sample size $\sqrt{n}$, not by $n$ itself.
Standard error decreases with sample size; divide by $\sqrt{n}$, do not multiply.
Standard error of the mean uses $\sqrt{n}$ in the denominator, not sample degrees of freedom $n - 1$.

stages.explanation_markdown: The standard error of the sample mean is $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{20.0}{\sqrt{25}} = \frac{20.0}{5} = 4.0\ \mu\text{m}$. Excel formula: `=20.0/SQRT(25)`.

stages.prompt_markdown: Calculate the new standard error $\sigma_{\bar{x}}$ after quadrupling the sample size to $n_2 = 100$ pins.

options.hint_markdown: Quadrupling $n$ reduces standard error by $\sqrt{4} = 2$, not by $4$.
Remember to take the square root of sample size: $\sqrt{100} = 10$, so $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = 20.0 / 10 = 2.0\ \mu\text{m}$.

options.text_markdown: $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = 4.0\ \mu\text{m}$ (standard error does not change with sample size)
options.hint_markdown: Standard error measures the precision of the sample mean and shrinks as sample size increases.

stages.explanation_markdown: With $n_2 = 100$, the new standard error is $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n_2}} = \frac{20.0}{\sqrt{100}} = \frac{20.0}{10} = 2.0\ \mu\text{m}$. Excel formula: `=20.0/SQRT(100)`.

stages.prompt_markdown: Why did a $4\times$ increase in sample size ($25 \to 100$) only cut the standard error in half ($4.0\ \mu\text{m} \to 2.0\ \mu\text{m}$) rather than reducing it by fourfold?

options.text_markdown: Because $\sigma_{\bar{x}}$ is inversely proportional to $\sqrt{n}$, multiplying $n$ by $4$ reduces standard error by a factor of $\sqrt{4} = 2$.
Statistical precision always scales linearly with sample size, but measurement error in machining prevents full gains.
options.hint_markdown: The mathematical formula itself has $\sqrt{n}$ in the denominator, establishing a square-root relationship rather than a linear one.

options.text_markdown: Increasing sample size changes the underlying population standard deviation $\sigma$, mitigating the reduction.
options.hint_markdown: The population standard deviation $\sigma$ is a fixed property of the physical manufacturing process and does not change when we take larger samples.

options.text_markdown: The finite population correction factor neutralized half of the sample size benefit.
options.hint_markdown: In continuous mass production of titanium pins, the population is effectively infinite, so the FPC factor is 1.0.

stages.explanation_markdown: The standard error formula $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ illustrates the 'square-root law' of sampling precision: to cut standard error in half, sample size must increase by $2^2 = 4\times$. To cut it to one-tenth, sample size must increase by $10^2 = 100\times$. This reflects the diminishing marginal return of collecting larger samples.
